issues.legal_issue: Ownership of property cannot be awarded on the basis of adverse possession when that basis was neither pleaded nor made an issue for trial.
material_facts: The claimant sued for a declaration of ownership and a permanent injunction concerning land.
The trial court found that the claimant had purchased the land and also declared him owner by adverse possession, although he had not pleaded adverse possession and no issue on it had been framed.
The first appellate court found that the claimant had not proved the purchase and set aside the decree; the High Court affirmed that decision.
The Supreme Court endorsed the appellate courts’ findings and held that the trial court’s decree based on adverse possession was erroneous and unsustainable.
issues.conclusion: The claimant could not obtain a declaration of ownership on an adverse-possession basis that he had not pleaded and that had not been framed as an issue; the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: A claim of adverse possession is a blended question of fact and law and requires proper pleading and proof; a prayer or finding cannot substitute for a plea identifying when possession became adverse. The Court relied on S.M. Karim v. Bibi Sakina, R. Chandevarappa v. State of Karnataka, D.N. Venkatarayappa v. State of Karnataka, Md. Mohammad Ali v. Jagadish Kalita, and Karnataka Board of Wakf v. Government of India.

predicates.civil_appeal_from_title_suit: A party brought a civil appeal arising from a suit seeking a declaration of ownership over property.
predicates.adverse_possession_not_pleaded: The claimant did not plead that the claimant had acquired ownership through adverse possession.
predicates.no_adverse_possession_issue_framed: The trial court did not frame an issue for determination on whether ownership had been acquired through adverse possession.

issues.definition: When a civil appeal arises from a property-title suit and adverse possession was neither pleaded nor made an issue for trial, ownership cannot be awarded on that basis.

issues.legal_issue: A person claiming ownership by adverse possession must prove possession that is open, continuous, peaceful, and hostile to the true owner, together with the intention to possess adversely and facts establishing when the possession became adverse.
material_facts: The claimant asserted ownership of the land, while the trial court described possession extending over many years and also found that the claimant had forcibly taken possession in 1960 and remained in possession until 1986.
The claimant did not plead adverse possession, and no issue on that basis was framed.

The first appellate court and the High Court found that the claimant had failed to establish title; the Supreme Court endorsed their findings and held that he had not established title by adverse possession.
issues.conclusion: The claimant failed to establish that he had perfected title by adverse possession.
issues.legal_principle: Adverse possession must be nec vi, nec clam, nec precario and adequate in continuity, publicity, and extent; it must be actual, visible, exclusive, hostile, and continued for the applicable statutory period. The claimant must establish the nature and duration of possession, that it was open and known or capable of being known to the owner, the hostile claim and animus possidendi, and when the possession became adverse. The Court relied on Secretary of State for India v. Debendra Lal Khan, P. Lakshmi Reddy v. L. Lakshmi Reddy, S.M. Karim v. Bibi Sakina, R. Chandevarappa v. State of Karnataka, D.N. Venkatarayappa v. State of Karnataka, Md. Mohammad Ali v. Jagadish Kalita, Karnataka Board of Wakf v. Government of India, Saroop Singh v. Banto, M. Durai v. Muthu, T. Anjanappa v. Somalingappa, and P.T. Munichikkanna Reddy v. Revamma. The Court discussed Article 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963, and Articles 142 and 144 of the former Limitation Act.

rule.if: civil_appeal_from_title_suit and adverse_possession_claim and (not hostile_possession_proven or not open_continuous_possession_proven or not animus_possidendi_proven or not adverse_starting_point_identified)

predicates.civil_appeal_from_title_suit: A party brought a civil appeal arising from a suit seeking a declaration of ownership over property.
predicates.adverse_possession_claim: A claimant relies on possession as the basis for acquiring ownership against the true owner.
predicates.hostile_possession_proven: The claimant proved possession asserting a hostile title in denial of the true owner’s title.
predicates.open_continuous_possession_proven: The claimant proved possession that was open and continuous for the required period.
predicates.animus_possidendi_proven: The claimant proved an intention to possess the property adversely to the true owner.
predicates.adverse_starting_point_identified: The claimant identified when possession became adverse so that the start of the applicable limitation period could be determined.

issues.definition: In a civil appeal from a title suit, a claim based on adverse possession does not establish ownership if the claimant fails to prove any required feature of adverse possession or to identify when it became adverse.
